# Links to the Sources

The first dataset about pollution per counties in the United States, was published by The Environmental Protection agency and more precisely measured by the Air Quality System (AQS). It's measure system is based on a monitor located in most counties which measures different pollution levels and metrics (ozone, carbone monoxyde ...). Instead of a precise device a monitor represent a place where a parameter is being measure at a given site.

The second element of our study is a group of datasets representing different measures of socio-economic features in all counties of the US. These measures were collected by the American community survey and more precisely by the Census Bureau and are published every year and is of the most reliable information source about societey characteristics in America.

## Variables

Median household income in the past 12 months (inflation adjusted dollars) : This is a quite explicit variable, it’s a very straightforward way to measure wealth in each county and we picked it over mean because it is not skewed  by high incomes. One limit is that there are margins of error because these are survey data (note that the margins of error rarely exceed 10 000usd for annual income).

Unemployment rate : This is a variable we’re going to compute manually (dividing the unemployed population over the total labor force of the county), it’s another very useful measure and we could observe if there exists higher or lower exposition to pollution when the county is more or less employed. This also interesting because maybe some counties are more industrial and have higher employment rate but also higher pollution exposition.

Ozone measured with arithmetic mean of 8hour average  2015 standard as reference in parts per million, we chose this variable to partly represent pollution in counties because first of all it’s the widest pollutant measured on  monitors so it allows us to really have a vast view. But also it’s a very impacting gas for human health and is very present coming from vehicles and industry . We’re going to compare it to the 4th highest daily maximum, the official EPA measure for the ozone standard (0.070 ppm) set in 2015.

Another variable we will focus on is the annual arithmetic mean of long term exposure to PM25 particles (representing fine particulate matter). It’s the most harmful air pollutant especially causing heart and respiratory diseases. It comes from traffic, power plants and industrial production. There are less monitors measuring PM25 but there still are around 900 values observed in all the counties. We will directly compare it withe the EPA standard of 9µg/m^3.

The last variable about air pollution is Nitrogen dioxide in parts per billion, we will also measure it with its annual arithmetic mean. It comes mainly from road traffic and is concentrated in dense urban areas. That makes it the pollutant most directly tied to where people live and work, and the one most often used in environmental justice research. It also contributes to forming PM2.5 and ozone. This variable is less captured by monitors but it still very impactful so we want to keep

## ACS Data

```{r}

#| message: false
#| warning: false
education <- vroom(here("data", "education.csv"))
employment <- vroom(here("data", "employment.csv"))
ethnicity <- vroom(here("data", "ethnicity.csv"))
median_income <- vroom(here("data", "median_income.csv"))
population <- vroom(here("data", "population.csv"))

cleaning_ACS <- function(df){
  names(df)[2:ncol(df)] <- as.character(df[1, 2:ncol(df)])
  df <- df[-1, ] #explicit title is in line 1
  df <- df[, -ncol(df)] #always full of NA
  df[3:ncol(df)] <- lapply(df[3:ncol(df)], as.integer) #integer type for every column but 1 & 2
  df
}

education <- cleaning_ACS(education)
employment <- cleaning_ACS(employment)
ethnicity <- cleaning_ACS(ethnicity) |>
  select(!4) #full of NA
median_income <- cleaning_ACS(median_income)
population <- cleaning_ACS(population) |>
  select(!4) #full of NA
```

# Data joining and cleaning

## Separating state and county in ACS Data

In order to join the data, it is essential first to work with our key variable under the same format.

### Harmonizing State and County's name format

In EPA Data, we have two different columns County Name and State Name. In ACS Data, we have one unique column under the following form : County Name, State Name. We then have to split them by "," to obtain two different columns, in order to have the same form in both datasets. 

```{r}
sep_state_county_str <- function(df){
  df |> 
    separate_wider_delim(`Geographic Area Name`,
                         delim = ",",
                         names = c("County Name", "State Name"))
}

remove_county_suffix <- function(df){
  df$`County Name` <- str_remove(df$`County Name`, " County$")
  df
}
#$ sert à enlever " County" en fin de chaîne uniquement (plus sûr)

education <- education |>
  sep_state_county_str() |>
  remove_county_suffix()
employment <- employment |>
  sep_state_county_str() |>
  remove_county_suffix()
ethnicity <- ethnicity |>
  sep_state_county_str() |>
  remove_county_suffix()
median_income <- median_income |>
  sep_state_county_str() |>
  remove_county_suffix()
population <- population |>
  sep_state_county_str() |>
  remove_county_suffix()
```

### Harmonizing State and County's code format

In EPA Data, we have a State code and a County Code (1, 24 or 456 for instance). In ACS Data we have a unique geo_id where the five last numbers are the State code and the County Code in that order. Therefore, we have to extract these last 5 numbers from the geo_id, to split them and to turn 001 into 1 for instance. After mutating, we will have two new columns, one County Code and one State Code, with numbers as 1, 24 or 456 for instance : the format will be exactly the same between the two datasets.

```{r}
sep_county_state_code <- function(df){
  df |>
    mutate(`State Code` = as.integer(str_sub(GEO_ID, -5, -4)),
           `County Code` = as.integer(str_sub(GEO_ID, -3, -1)))
}
#-5 est le 5ème élément du geo_id en partant de la fin
#as.integer transforms 001 into 1 for instance

education <- sep_county_state_code(education)
employment <- sep_county_state_code(employment)
ethnicity <- sep_county_state_code(ethnicity)
median_income <- sep_county_state_code(median_income)
population <- sep_county_state_code(population)
```
